newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korea says sorry over submarine incursion.
newsitem.headline: North Korea says sorry over submarine incursion.

text.p: North Korea apologised for the first time on Sunday for an incursion by one of its submarines into South Korea in September, expressing "deep regret" in a statement that was hammered out with U.S. diplomats.
The statement, carried by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) and monitored in Tokyo, promised no repetitions of the incident.

South Korea, which received the text of the apology in advance, welcomed it as a chance to "wrap up the submarine incident" and said it suggested North Korea was ready to respond positively to an offer of peace talks.

"We hope that North Korea will use this opportunity to work for peace and stability on the Korean peninsula and will respond earnestly to our efforts to improve South-North relations," a government statement in Seoul said.

South Korea had demanded an apology as the price of resuming aid shipments and other contacts with the North and implementing a landmark agreement to supply its communist neighbour with nuclear reactors.
Out of 26 North Koreans that landed from the submarine which ran aground on an east coast beach, 24 were shot dead, one was captured alive and one is still on the loose.
There was no immediate word on whether Seoul would now respond to a North Korean demand for the return of the bodies of the infiltrators.

"The spokesman of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the DPRK is authorised to express deep regret for the submarine incident in the coastal waters of Kangnung, South Korea, in September, 1996, that caused the tragic loss of human life," KCNA said in a brief report.
"The DPRK will make efforts to ensure that such an incident will not recur and will work with others for durable peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula."
U.S. diplomats have been meeting North Korean envoys in New York this month to urge Pyongyang to make an apology that would satisfy Seoul. The latest session was on Friday.

The apology represents a major climb-down for Pyongyang that has previously threatened to relatiate "a hundredfold or a thousandfold" over the deaths of its agents. It vowed that "blood shall be paid with blood".
But analyts noted that the announcement, also broadcast over Pyongyang radio, would not have reached ordinary North Koreans. KCNA and Pyongyang radio are for overseas consumption only.

South Korean President Kim Young-sam condenmed the intrusion as a "military provocation" that violated a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War. He froze all contacts with the North and warned of "all-out war".

The South also suspended the implementation of a 1994 agreement between Washington and Pyongyang under which it will supply nuclear reactors to the North. The accord obliged Pyongyang to freeze its nuclear arms programme.

North Korea is on the verge of famine because of devastating floods and economic mismanagement and desperately needed to put the submarine crisis behind it so it could get further food aid from the United States.
It was not clear whether Washington secured the apology with any promises of aid or diplomatic recognition.
There have been hopes that an apology will open the way to four-party talks proposed by South Korea and the United States with the North and China on a lasting peace to replace the Korean armistice.
It may also allow further discussion on opening a U.S. diplomatic liaison office in Pyongyang, which has been bogged down over technical details.
